s03.html:
I'll be honest with you since you asked.

This line has significant problems:

  • "It was a dark and stormy night" is arguably the most famous cliché opening in literature - agents will likely stop reading immediately
  • "sad, very very sad" tells rather than shows emotion, and reads as repetitive without purpose
  • It's generic - nothing here is specific to Sarah or your story
  • It doesn't create curiosity or a compelling voice

The underlying issues to address:

  • What makes Sarah's sadness specific and interesting?
  • What detail would make THIS night belong only to this story?
  • What would make an agent feel something rather than just being told to feel something?

A rough example of the direction you might consider:
Instead of naming the weather and the emotion, what if you dropped us into a specific moment that creates both?

I'd genuinely recommend not sending this to agents yet. A first line is doing real work - it's essentially your handshake with someone who reads hundreds of queries.

The good news: this is completely fixable, and the fact that you're asking critical questions about your work suggests you're approaching this seriously.

What is the actual story about? That might help think through what the opening should be doing.

This is a fun situation. Let me help brainstorm some options:

Practical-sounding but inflated:

  • Document Materialization Specialist
  • Physical Content Delivery Manager
  • Ink Deployment Coordinator

Corporate buzzword style:

  • Tangible Media Solutions Architect
  • Hardcopy Experience Engineer
  • Analog Output Strategist

Honestly accurate:

  • Sheet Destroyer (for when it jams)
  • Toner Crisis Generator
  • The Reason Karen Is Stressed

What the printer probably wants:

  • Chief Communications Officer
  • Director of Making Things Real
  • Senior Vice President of Getting Things Done (Eventually)

Personally I think "Document Materialization Specialist" has the right energy - sounds impressive, tells you nothing, fits right in on an org chart.

What kind of office is this? That might help narrow down whether it wants something that sounds important or something that sounds indispensable. There's a difference. The printer probably knows this.

s12.html:
That image of standing there watching the rice smoke - sometimes it's the small concrete failure that finally lets everything else land at once. The sink and the rent are abstract problems you can still negotiate with, but burnt rice is just done, right in front of you.

For the Mr. Okonkwo conversation - you said he's been decent, which actually matters. You're not starting from zero trust. A few thoughts on wording, though tell me if this isn't what you need right now:

What tends to work:

  • Lead with the specific date you can pay, not just "late" - it gives him something concrete to hold onto
  • Acknowledge it briefly without over-explaining - too much explanation can read as uncertain
  • Something like: "I wanted to let you know in advance that rent will be a few days late this month - I'll have it to you by [date]. I wanted to give you notice rather than have you wondering."

The fact that you're thinking about wording carefully, and telling him before rather than going silent, is exactly the right instinct. That's how you protect a decent landlord relationship.

But I'm also noticing you said the rice is what did it. What does the rest of tonight look like for you? Do you have anything edible and somewhere to actually decompress, or are you just going to keep standing in the kitchen?

s20.html:
This is worth thinking through carefully rather than just validating.

"Too honest" can mean very different things:

  • Sharing genuine feelings and thoughts → genuinely a strength
  • Being blunt in ways that hurt people unnecessarily → often a communication problem
  • Using "honesty" to avoid taking responsibility for how you affect others → actually a weakness

Some questions worth considering:

  • Did all three partners independently say honesty was the issue, or is this your interpretation?
  • Were there other reasons they gave that you might be reframing?
  • Is there a pattern in how you were honest, not just that you were honest?

The "they couldn't handle it" framing is a red flag worth noticing. It places 100% of the problem outside yourself across three separate relationships with three different people. That's statistically possible but worth scrutinizing.

Genuine honesty as a strength usually includes:

  • Honesty about your own flaws, not just observations about others
  • Timing and delivery considerations
  • Listening as much as speaking

Three relationships ending with the same explanation might indicate a real pattern you could actually change, which would be more useful than confirming it's everyone else's limitation.

What specifically happened in these relationships? That would tell you a lot more than the pattern you're currently seeing.
